items.title: Make the two-stick control grammar readable at a glance
items.what: On the portrait fight screen, the lower half is dominated by two large, nearly identical circular pads. The small panel immediately above them says "STANCE" and "TECHNIQUE" with lines such as "◄ step ▲ jump" and "◄ back ► forward," but the text and arrow meanings are tiny relative to the controls and the relationship between a stick direction and a resulting attack is not obvious.
items.why: This is the core interaction a new player must understand in the first seconds. A player can see two expensive-looking touch pads but still has to decipher whether they drag, tap, combine, or select directions, increasing failed inputs before the first exchange.
items.how: Add a first-bout, dismissible control callout directly over the pads: label the left pad "MOVE / STANCE" and the right pad "ATTACK DIRECTION," animate one short example path, and show the resulting move name (for example, "Right + Forward = Lunge Punch"). Increase the instructional panel's type size and replace the tiny textual arrows with the same high-contrast directional icons used inside each pad.

items.title: Remove the conflict between the Fight button and auto-start countdown
items.what: The Qualifier pre-fight screen presents a large gold button labeled "FIGHT," while directly beneath it the screen says "STARTING IN 2," "STARTING IN 3," or "STARTING IN 4." The screenshot gives two contradictory signals: tap now, or wait for an automatic start.
items.why: A prominent button is a promise of agency. When a bout starts anyway, a first-time player may either hesitate instead of preparing their thumbs or repeatedly tap a control that appears unnecessary.
items.how: Choose one primary behavior. If the bout auto-starts, replace the button with a non-interactive countdown treatment such as "GET READY — 3" and show a small "Tap to start now" secondary option. If tapping is required, remove "Starting in" and change the label to "Tap Fight to Begin."

items.title: Give the fighters more of the portrait combat frame
items.what: In the active portrait fight screenshots, the area between the HUD and the shoji windows is a large empty field of dark ceiling/light haze, while both fighters begin around the middle-lower region. Their heads sit roughly halfway down the arena, and the meaningful combat space is visually compressed between that dead headroom and the control legend.
items.why: On a phone, opponent posture, limb motion, and hit distance need to be instantly readable. The current framing spends substantial vertical space on atmosphere while making the photoreal fighter silhouettes and attack separation smaller than they need to be.
items.how: For portrait gameplay, move the camera crop down and zoom the combat layer approximately 10–15%, keeping both feet and a safe side margin visible. Preserve the warm dojo background, but reduce the empty upper dojo area and reserve that reclaimed space for brief combat feedback.

items.title: Explain points where the player sees the hit
items.what: The hit screenshot shows a large "IPPON" callout and a smaller "SPINNING BACK KICK" label, while the top-right score changes to "1." Elsewhere, the Moves screen lists outcomes as "Half point" and "Full point," and the loss screen shows the unusual score "0 — 2½." None of the combat-facing screens visibly explains how IPPON, move type, and full/half-point score increments relate.
items.why: Players cannot form a reliable strategy if they do not know why a strike earned 1, ½, or a match-winning total. The half-point notation is especially easy to miss in the compact red HUD score.
items.how: On every confirmed score, show a single unified result near the impact, for example "IPPON +1" or "WAZA-ARI +½," then briefly animate the same increment into the scorer's HUD number. Add a one-line explanation on the Qualifier screen or first Moves view: "Clean attacks score ½ or 1 point; first to the round target wins."

items.title: Make the branded loading state feel visibly alive
items.what: The ShoeMoney pre-boot screen is mostly near-black empty space with a centered logo and a very thin brown progress track. The text only says "Downloading the game," and the fill/progress state is not clearly distinguishable from the track in the screenshot.
items.why: This is the product's first visible screen. On a mobile connection, an indistinct bar can look stalled, encouraging early abandonment before players ever reach the dojo.
items.how: Keep the restrained dark brand treatment, but use a clearly brighter gold fill against the track, animate a subtle indeterminate shimmer before measurable progress is available, and display a compact numerical status such as "Downloading dojo assets 62%" or "Preparing fighters…" beneath the bar.
